content: A cigarillo, derived from the Spanish word for cigarette and pronounced see-gah-ree-yoh in Spanish or see-gah-ree-loh in English, is a small, narrow cigar. Unlike cigarettes, cigarillos are wrapped in whole-leaf tobacco rather than paper. They typically contain fewer additives compared to cigarettes, though they often have more additives than traditional cigars. Cigarillos are available for purchase individually or in packs and are sometimes produced without filters. Filtered cigarillos are occasionally referred to as little cigars. Unlike cigarettes, cigarillos are not intended to be inhaled but are instead smoked in a manner similar to cigars. Cigarillos are generally 8 cm in length and 5 to 8 mm in diameter. In comparison, cigarettes are less than 12 cm long, less than 1 cm in diameter, and contain less than 1 gram of tobacco. Cigarillos are often machine-made, which reduces their cost compared to handmade cigars. While they are not produced in the same large quantities as cigarettes, cigarillos are sometimes viewed by dedicated cigar smokers as a lower-quality product. Since cigarillos are often smoked in quantities similar to cigarettes (5 to 10 per day), they typically do not require storage in humidors. In Europe, they are sometimes referred to as Seven Minute Cigars because they can be smoked in approximately seven minutes, making them a convenient alternative for those who lack the time to smoke a full-sized cigar. To enhance their appeal, cigarillos are often sold in decorative tins. Manufacturers claim that these tins provide better protection against crushing, but they also improve the product's image and allow for more targeted marketing to individuals who are conscious of how their smoking habits are perceived by others. In the United States, popular cigarillo brands include Swisher Sweets, Black and Mild, White Owl, Optimo, and Winchester. In the United Kingdom, brands such as Hamlets and Café Crème are well-known. Inexpensive cigarillos are often identified by their brand names rather than the term cigarillo. In Europe, cigarillos and thin panatelas (long, slender cigars) are relatively more popular among female smokers, possibly because it is still socially less acceptable or surprising to see women smoking larger cigars. Health Concerns As with other tobacco products, cigarillos pose health risks to those who smoke them. In Europe, they are subject to regulations requiring health warnings to be displayed on a portion of the packaging. Since cigarillos are not intended to be inhaled, they are sometimes perceived as a healthier alternative to cigarettes. However, health authorities worldwide caution smokers about the risks associated with having smoke in the mouth, as this still poses significant health concerns. Taxation In the United States, cigarillos (and cigars) are taxed at a lower rate than cigarettes. The federal tax on cigarettes is 39 cents per pack, whereas cigarillos are taxed at 4 cents per pack of 20. Large cigars are subject to a maximum federal tax of 5 cents per cigar. Some states impose no tax on cigarillos at all.
